title: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java 8+, and when does the choice between them actually matter?
shortTitle: Abstract class vs interface in Java 8+ — when does the choice actually matter?

s1_definition.profdef: Since Java 8, interfaces can have `default` methods (with body) and `static` methods, making them MORE powerful than pre-Java-8. The remaining differences: (1) STATE: abstract class CAN have instance fields (state); interface can only have `public static final` constants. (2) CONSTRUCTORS: abstract class CAN have constructors; interface CANNOT. (3) SINGLE vs MULTIPLE: a class can extend ONLY ONE abstract class but implement MULTIPLE interfaces. (4) ACCESS: abstract class methods can be any access modifier; interface methods are implicitly public (private since Java 9 for helper methods). The choice matters when: you NEED state or constructors → abstract class. You NEED multiple inheritance of behavior → interface. You're defining a CAPABILITY (Comparable, Serializable) → interface. You're defining a PARTIAL implementation with shared state (template method pattern) → abstract class. In modern Java, prefer interfaces with default methods; use abstract classes only when you need shared mutable state.
s1_definition.analogy: INTERFACE is like a banking LICENSE: "Any institution that implements `DepositService` must provide `deposit()` and `withdraw()`." A bank, a payment app, and a cooperative — all can hold this license (implement the interface). Multiple licenses allowed. ABSTRACT CLASS is like a BANK TEMPLATE: "All branches share this common code (balance tracking, audit logging), but each branch fills in its own interest rate." Only ONE template per branch (single inheritance). The template HAS state (balance field) and a constructor (initializes accountId). The license (interface) does NOT have state.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface = contract + multiple inheritance + no state. Abstract class = partial implementation + single inheritance + CAN have state/constructors. Modern Java: prefer interface with default methods. Use abstract class when you need shared mutable fields.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Since Java 8, interfaces can have `default` methods (with body) and `static` methods, making them MORE powerful than pre-Java-8. The remaining differences: (1) STATE: abstract class CAN have instance fields (state); interface can only have `public static final` constants. (2) CONSTRUCTORS: abstract class CAN have constructors; interface CANNOT. (3) SINGLE vs MULTIPLE: a class can extend ONLY ONE abstract class but implement MULTIPLE interfaces. (4) ACCESS: abstract class methods can be any access modifier; interface methods are implicitly public (private since Java 9 for helper methods). The choice matters when: you NEED state or constructors → abstract class. You NEED multiple inheritance of behavior → interface. You're defining a CAPABILITY (Comparable, Serializable) → interface. You're defining a PARTIAL implementation with shared state (template method pattern) → abstract class. In modern Java, prefer interfaces with default methods; use abstract classes only when you need shared mutable state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** INTERFACE is like a banking LICENSE: "Any institution that implements `DepositService` must provide `deposit()` and `withdraw()`." A bank, a payment app, and a cooperative — all can hold this license (implement the interface). Multiple licenses allowed. ABSTRACT CLASS is like a BANK TEMPLATE: "All branches share this common code (balance tracking, audit logging), but each branch fills in its own interest rate." Only ONE template per branch (single inheritance). The template HAS state (balance field) and a constructor (initializes accountId). The license (interface) does NOT have state.

**One line to remember:** Interface = contract + multiple inheritance + no state. Abstract class = partial implementation + single inheritance + CAN have state/constructors. Modern Java: prefer interface with default methods. Use abstract class when you need shared mutable fields.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank needs to model accounts AND cross-cutting capabilities.** Account is a TYPE HIERARCHY: SavingsAccount IS-A Account, CurrentAccount IS-A Account. They share state (balance, accountId, auditLog) and behavior (deposit, withdraw). This is an abstract class. Additionally, some accounts are Auditable (generates audit reports), some are Notifiable (sends SMS on transactions), some are Transferable (can transfer to other accounts). These are CAPABILITIES — not all accounts have all of them. A SavingsAccount is Auditable + Notifiable but NOT Transferable (can't transfer directly). A CurrentAccount is Auditable + Notifiable + Transferable. These capabilities are interfaces — a class can implement MULTIPLE.

**What the project will show:** Abstract class Account with shared state + constructor + template method, three interfaces (Auditable, Notifiable, Transferable), SavingsAccount extends Account implements Auditable + Notifiable, CurrentAccount extends Account implements ALL THREE, and why each decision was made.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Abstract class provides state.** `new SavingsAccount("SAV2001", 120000, 0.04)` calls `super(accountId, initialBalance)` — the abstract Account constructor initializes accountId, balance, and auditLog. Interface CANNOT do this — no constructors, no instance fields.

**Step 2 — Template method uses abstract method.** `savings.processMonthEnd()` is a CONCRETE method in Account that calls `calculateInterest()` — an ABSTRACT method implemented by SavingsAccount (returns 400). The template method pattern: the algorithm is in the parent, the specific step is in the child.

**Step 3 — Interfaces provide capabilities.** SavingsAccount implements Auditable + Notifiable. CurrentAccount implements Auditable + Notifiable + Transferable. Only CurrentAccount can transfer — SavingsAccount doesn't have the Transferable capability. Multiple interfaces = selective capabilities.

**Step 4 — Capability-based processing.** `allAccounts.stream().filter(a -> a instanceof Transferable)` — only CurrentAccount passes. `((Transferable) a).transferTo(...)` — processes only accounts WITH the transfer capability. Interface enables this capability-based filtering.

**Step 5 — Why BOTH are needed.** Account (abstract class): shared state (balance), constructor, template method. Cannot be replaced by interface. Auditable/Notifiable/Transferable (interfaces): cross-cutting capabilities, multiple inheritance, no state needed. Cannot be replaced by abstract class (single inheritance limit). The system needs BOTH.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ABSTRACT CLASS vs INTERFACE — WHEN TO USE ═══

  ABSTRACT CLASS (Account):               INTERFACE (Auditable, Notifiable):
  ├─ HAS instance fields (balance)         ├─ NO instance fields (constants only)
  ├─ HAS constructors                      ├─ NO constructors
  ├─ Single inheritance ONLY               ├─ Multiple implementation ✅
  ├─ Template method pattern               ├─ Default methods (Java 8+)
  ├─ IS-A relationship (noun)              ├─ HAS-A capability (adjective)
  └─ "SavingsAccount IS-A Account"         └─ "SavingsAccount IS Auditable"

  ═══ DECISION RULES ═══

  Need shared mutable state?      → abstract class
  Need constructors?              → abstract class
  Need multiple inheritance?      → interface
  Defining a capability?          → interface
  Defining a type hierarchy?      → abstract class
  Don't need state?               → interface (modern default)

  ═══ COMBINED USAGE ═══

  class SavingsAccount extends Account implements Auditable, Notifiable {
       │                        │                    │
       ONE abstract class       MULTIPLE interfaces
       (state + template)       (capabilities)
  }
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Since Java 8, the feature gap between abstract class and interface has narrowed — interfaces now have default methods, static methods, and private methods. The remaining differences that drive the choice: abstract classes CAN have instance fields and constructors (shared mutable state); interfaces CANNOT. A class can extend only ONE abstract class but implement MULTIPLE interfaces. Use abstract class when you need shared state across subclasses (balance field, audit log) and a constructor to initialize it (template method pattern). Use interface when you define a capability (Auditable, Serializable, Comparable) that multiple unrelated classes may need.

In my account capability service, Account is an abstract class because it has shared mutable state (balance, auditLog), a constructor (initializes accountId + balance), and a template method (processMonthEnd calls calculateInterest → deposit). This CANNOT be an interface. Auditable, Notifiable, and Transferable are interfaces because: SavingsAccount needs Auditable + Notifiable (2 interfaces), CurrentAccount needs all three (3 interfaces), and a single abstract class inheritance slot is already used by Account. Multiple inheritance of capabilities is only possible with interfaces.

The modern Java guideline: prefer interfaces with default methods as your first choice. Resort to abstract class only when you need shared mutable instance fields or constructors. Don't "waste" the single inheritance slot — a class can implement unlimited interfaces but extend only one class. In Spring, JpaRepository is an interface (classes can implement multiple repositories). Controllers extend no abstract class (they implement interfaces or are standalone). The Template Method Pattern (abstract class with abstract + concrete methods) is the primary use case for abstract classes in modern Java.
